taxonomyNote: NatureServe recognizes four subspecies (ruber, nitidus, schencki, vioscai) that Folt et al. (2016) found are not monophyletic lineages.
fieldMarks: Bright orange-red to red above with scattered black spots; black chin; short tail; about 16 body grooves; 11-18 cm.
Older adults fade to purplish-brown with larger spots.
Larvae purplish-brown above with a yellowish underside and black spots.
Yellow iris and longer snout than the mud salamander.
behavior: Mainly nocturnal; adults move from streams to terrestrial shelter in spring and return in late summer or fall to breed.
Eats aquatic and terrestrial insects, earthworms, snails, slugs, spiders and small salamanders; larvae eat aquatic flies and crustaceans.
Larval stage lasts 18-33 months; females lay 50-100 eggs in fall under rocks in water; aposematic coloration resembles the toxic eastern newt.
habitat: Cold, clear, rocky streams and springs in wooded or open areas; adults in leaf litter, under rocks and in crevices and burrows near water, sometimes in caves.
range: Eastern United States from New York south along the Appalachians to the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, Alabama and the western Florida panhandle; absent from the Coastal Plain of Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. NatureServe lists a Canadian national record (CA), but no Canadian range was sourced.

lookalikes.name: Mud salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: Mud salamander has brown eyes and a shorter snout; red salamander has a yellow iris.

lookalikes.name: Eastern newt
lookalikes.howToTell: Newt skin is rough and lacks prominent grooves; red salamander has about 16 grooves and a black chin.
